style_when: the article explains how a system, process or stack actually works — money flows, supply chains, pipelines, an agent assembly line
prompt: Clean isometric cutaway illustration of an automated warehouse aisle on a polished concrete floor. A fleet of identical unbranded autonomous mobile robots is arranged in a rigid symmetrical grid, rows receding toward a far steel rack where one blank paper invoice lies. Each robot has a matte grey polymer chassis with safety-yellow trim, black drive wheels, and visible battery bay seams. One directional hard light from the upper left casts long shadows across the concrete. Graphite, bone white, and safety yellow palette. Thin consistent line weight, unlabelled, generous empty margin, one-point perspective down the aisle.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, signatures, logos
rationale: The story is structural and systemic—how a fleet ages together and produces a single unbudgeted replacement bill. A technical isometric cutaway can show the fleet as a physical grid while keeping the blank invoice as a recognizable artifact, avoiding a sterile datacenter or office stock.
cue: the second purchase is a capital plan
subject: a fleet of identical unbranded autonomous mobile robots in a warehouse aisle with a blank paper invoice on a steel rack
core_thesis: A robot fleet bought in one year comes back as a single renewal bill about eight times the annual charge, and a reserve funded at the original invoice covers only about three quarters of the replacement price once the equipment index compounds across an 8.3-year life.
core_conflict: The governing tension is between a one-time capital outlay spread across an original schedule and the compounded replacement cost that arrives as one unscheduled wave when the entire fleet ages together.
composition: isometric cutaway with symmetrical grid and one off-centre invoice on a steel rack, one-point perspective down the aisle
